regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Lung settings: previously treated NSCLC; first-line PD-L1-high metastatic NSCLC; adjuvant NSCLC after surgery and platinum chemotherapy; ES-SCLC maintenance after induction.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Atezolizumab: Atezolizumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can help cancer cells evade immune attack. Blocking PD-L1 can help immune cells attack cancer, but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: Atezolizumab 1200 mg is given by intravenous infusion on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). The first infusion lasts about 60 minutes; later infusions may last 30 minutes if tolerated. The visit includes checks and preparation. This protocol also offers a separately prescribed 1875 mg injection under the skin of the thigh over about 7 minutes every 3 weeks. The IV and under-skin doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Adjuvant: maximum 12 months. Advanced NSCLC and ES-SCLC maintenance: until progression or unacceptable toxicity. ES-SCLC requires completed induction; this suite contains no induction chemotherapy.
key_points: No atezolizumab dose reduction; use organ-specific hold/stop and restart rules.
Do not infer immune hepatitis/nephritis from isolated laboratory abnormalities.
Thyroid every 3–6 weeks regardless of infusion interval.
No routine cytotoxic antiemetic prophylaxis for monotherapy.

treatment_rationale.summary: Atezolizumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can help cancer cells evade immune attack. Blocking PD-L1 can help immune cells attack cancer, but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.
treatment_rationale.setting: Lung settings: previously treated NSCLC; first-line PD-L1-high metastatic NSCLC; adjuvant NSCLC after surgery and platinum chemotherapy; ES-SCLC maintenance after induction.
treatment_rationale.line: Post-platinum, first-line metastatic, adjuvant, or SCLC maintenance: confirm indication
factors: First-line metastatic NSCLC requires PD-L1 ≥50% tumour cells or ≥10% immune cells and no EGFR/ALK alteration. After prior chemotherapy, NSCLC has separate eligibility. Adjuvant use requires completely resected high-risk stage II–IIIA AJCC7, predominantly non-squamous cancer, PD-L1 ≥50%, no EGFR/ALK alteration and prior platinum chemotherapy. ES-SCLC use is maintenance after completed combination induction.
ECOG 0–1. Adjuvant platinum must commence within 12 weeks of surgery and atezolizumab within 12 weeks of the last platinum dose; no progression after chemotherapy.

First-line metastatic: no previous systemic treatment for stage IV disease; previous perioperative chemotherapy requires treatment-free interval ≥6 months. Post-chemotherapy NSCLC requires prior platinum and appropriate EGFR/ALK targeted treatment where relevant.

Symptomatic CNS metastases, hypersensitivity and clinically significant active infection are source exclusions. Symptomatic ILD and medical conditions requiring immunosuppression >10 mg/day prednisolone equivalent are source exclusions. Inhaled/topical steroids are excluded from that definition; autoimmune disease and previous checkpoint treatment require individual review.
alternatives: Consider setting-specific systemic therapy, targeted agents, clinical trials, surveillance and supportive care.
limitations: OAK, IMpower110, IMpower010 and IMpower133 used 1200 mg IV every 3 weeks. The 840 mg every 2 weeks, 1680 mg every 4 weeks and SC schedules rely on pharmacokinetic/formulation bridging, not separate head-to-head efficacy trials.
IMpower010 subgroup results are exploratory, unstratified PD-L1 ≥50%, EGFR/ALK-negative stage II–IIIA (n=209). Final DFS and second interim OS are not confirmatory overall-population OS results.
IMpower110 updated high-PD-L1 exploratory OS confidence interval crosses 1; distinguish it from the earlier positive primary analysis.
IMpower133 evaluates four-cycle combination induction followed by maintenance; it does not estimate the isolated benefit of maintenance alone.

Non-lung urothelial indications remain in the clinical protocol. This patient suite is lung-only; lung outcomes must not be used as urothelial evidence. Current access must be checked separately from trial evidence and licensing.

regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: Durvalumab is given after definitive chemoradiotherapy to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning or worsening and improve the chance of longer survival. This is part of a treatment pathway that aims for long-term control and possible cure; it cannot guarantee cure.
regimen_profiles.treatment_setting: Stage III NSCLC · consolidation after concurrent chemoradiotherapy
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Durvalumab binds PD-L1 and blocks its interaction with PD-1/CD80, supporting antitumour immune activity. It is given after the completed definitive concurrent CRT phase; its toxicity rules do not assess the earlier cytotoxic or radiation treatment.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: Durvalumab is infused on Day 1 of each 14-day cycle. The course lasts up to 12 months (26 cycles), and can finish earlier if the cancer progresses or side effects make continuation unsuitable. The first dose should start within 42 days after chemoradiotherapy finishes.
key_points: Consolidation for unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with no cancer progression and tumour PD-L1 of at least 1%.

Durvalumab is infused on Day 1 of each 14-day cycle. The course lasts up to 12 months (26 cycles), and can finish earlier if the cancer progresses or side effects make continuation unsuitable. The first dose should start within 42 days after chemoradiotherapy finishes.
The usual reference dose is 10 mg/kg, given into a vein over about 60 minutes every 14 days. Allow extra time for the clinical review, tests and preparation.
Dose escalation/reduction is not recommended for toxicity; use hold/discontinue rules and specialist management.
New pulmonary symptoms after CRT require distinction among radiation pneumonitis, immune pneumonitis, infection and progression.
Source Table 1 is CTCAE4.03; stable treated hypothyroidism/type1 diabetes does not share the blanket hold rule for unstable hyperthyroid/adrenal/pituitary disease.

Hepatic footnote b: with AST/ALT >3×ULN and bilirubin >2×ULN, investigate attribution. A confirmed alternative cause invokes AST/ALT-only recommendations; unknown attribution requires a hold/review. Independent AST/ALT >10×ULN or other-organ permanent stops remain applicable.

treatment_rationale.summary: Durvalumab is given after definitive chemoradiotherapy to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning or worsening and improve the chance of longer survival. This is part of a treatment pathway that aims for long-term control and possible cure; it cannot guarantee cure.
treatment_rationale.setting: Consolidation for unresectable stage III non-small-cell lung cancer after concurrent platinum chemotherapy and radiotherapy, with no cancer progression and tumour PD-L1 of at least 1%.
treatment_rationale.line: Consolidation after definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy in a curative-intent stage III pathway; not metastatic first-line monotherapy.
factors: Confirm NCCP eligibility, PD-L1 testing, performance status, CRT details and recovery.
Balance durable control and survival evidence against post-radiation lung risk, immune adverse events, pre-existing disease and patient preferences.
Agree route, interval, maximum duration, test ownership, emergency contact and access/reimbursement.
alternatives: Individual alternatives, observation or another treatment pathway require multidisciplinary review of stage, biomarkers, CRT recovery, comorbidity and patient preferences; no cross-trial ranking is implied.
limitations: These NCCP codes cover post-concurrent-CRT consolidation for unresectable stage III NSCLC. They do not cover sequential CRT, resectable perioperative NSCLC, metastatic combination treatment or small-cell lung cancer, even though EMA lists other durvalumab indications.

Current NCCP eligibility requires PD-L1 ≥1%, ECOG 0–1, at least two concurrent platinum cycles, radiation ≥60 Gy, and no progression. PACIFIC enrolled irrespective of PD-L1; overall-trial results are not a PD-L1 ≥1% subgroup estimate.

PD-L1 subgroup analyses were exploratory/post hoc for the 1% threshold, with tissue unavailable for some patients and small subgroups. They cannot establish benefit or no benefit for an individual or replace NCCP eligibility.
PACIFIC directly studied durvalumab every two weeks after concurrent chemoradiotherapy. This guide uses that interval.

The numerical OS/PFS results below come from the same exploratory five-year update with data cutoff 11 January 2021. They are not mixed with the original co-primary endpoint analyses or presented as individual benefit.
NCCP Table 1 explicitly uses CTCAE 4.03. Confirm the event-specific grade and alternative causes; general interface CTCAE5 aids are not a substitute for this source standard.

Current source hepatitis rows hold AST/ALT >3 through ≤10×ULN; the merged table cell includes >5–10. Stop above 10×ULN, bilirubin >3×ULN, or concurrent AST/ALT >3 and bilirubin >2 without an alternative cause. Do not copy another checkpoint inhibitor’s threshold.

General restart criteria require recovery to grade ≤1, steroid dose ≤10 mg/day prednisone equivalent and resumption within 12 weeks. Organ-specific permanent-stop rules take precedence. Controlled hormone-replacement endocrinopathies have a stated exception to the general severe/recurrent immune-event stop rule.
No durvalumab dose-reduction ladder is recommended for toxicity. Mild/moderate baseline renal or hepatic impairment requires no dose adjustment; data in severe impairment are limited.

Regular endocrine and organ-function monitoring is required; the NCCP source does not prescribe a routine trastuzumab-style cardiac imaging schedule. New cardiac symptoms require targeted urgent assessment.
Omitted inputs remain unassessed; a reassuring single domain does not authorise treatment. Source reconciliation and software checks are not independent consultant/pharmacy approval.

Radiation inflammation, immune inflammation, infection and cancer can cause similar symptoms. Report new or worsening breathing symptoms promptly so the team can assess the cause. Do not assume a new cough is only an old radiotherapy effect.

Thyroid, adrenal or diabetes problems may need hormone replacement or insulin, sometimes long term. Keep taking prescribed medicines and attend blood tests even when you feel well. Sudden severe weakness, vomiting, faintness, unusual thirst or drowsiness need urgent advice.

PD-L1 subgroup analyses were exploratory/post hoc for the 1% threshold, with tissue unavailable for some patients and small subgroups. They cannot establish benefit or no benefit for an individual or replace NCCP eligibility.

No durvalumab dose-reduction ladder is recommended for toxicity. Mild/moderate baseline renal or hepatic impairment requires no dose adjustment; data in severe impairment are limited.

limitations: These NCCP codes cover post-concurrent-CRT consolidation for unresectable stage III NSCLC. They do not cover sequential CRT, resectable perioperative NSCLC, metastatic combination treatment or small-cell lung cancer, even though EMA lists other durvalumab indications.

Current NCCP eligibility requires PD-L1 ≥1%, ECOG 0–1, at least two concurrent platinum cycles, radiation ≥60 Gy, and no progression. PACIFIC enrolled irrespective of PD-L1; overall-trial results are not a PD-L1 ≥1% subgroup estimate.

PD-L1 subgroup analyses were exploratory/post hoc for the 1% threshold, with tissue unavailable for some patients and small subgroups. They cannot establish benefit or no benefit for an individual or replace NCCP eligibility.

PACIFIC studied durvalumab every two weeks. The every-four-week schedule is supported by regulatory drug-exposure bridging; PACIFIC did not directly compare these two schedules or test this fixed dose as its randomised treatment.

For body weight ≤30 kg, NCCP requires 10 mg/kg every two weeks OR 20 mg/kg every four weeks until weight is >30 kg. The clinician must select and prescribe the interval; the fixed-dose card is not an automatic weight-based calculation.

The numerical OS/PFS results below come from the same exploratory five-year update with data cutoff 11 January 2021. They are not mixed with the original co-primary endpoint analyses or presented as individual benefit.
NCCP Table 1 explicitly uses CTCAE 4.03. Confirm the event-specific grade and alternative causes; general interface CTCAE5 aids are not a substitute for this source standard.

Current source hepatitis rows hold AST/ALT >3 through ≤10×ULN; the merged table cell includes >5–10. Stop above 10×ULN, bilirubin >3×ULN, or concurrent AST/ALT >3 and bilirubin >2 without an alternative cause. Do not copy another checkpoint inhibitor’s threshold.

General restart criteria require recovery to grade ≤1, steroid dose ≤10 mg/day prednisone equivalent and resumption within 12 weeks. Organ-specific permanent-stop rules take precedence. Controlled hormone-replacement endocrinopathies have a stated exception to the general severe/recurrent immune-event stop rule.
No durvalumab dose-reduction ladder is recommended for toxicity. Mild/moderate baseline renal or hepatic impairment requires no dose adjustment; data in severe impairment are limited.

Regular endocrine and organ-function monitoring is required; the NCCP source does not prescribe a routine trastuzumab-style cardiac imaging schedule. New cardiac symptoms require targeted urgent assessment.
Omitted inputs remain unassessed; a reassuring single domain does not authorise treatment. Source reconciliation and software checks are not independent consultant/pharmacy approval.

The 2026 PACIFIC-R five-year report is an uncontrolled observational early-access cohort, including sequential CRT and PD-L1 <1% patients. It provides real-world context but cannot replace the randomised PACIFIC comparison or broaden these NCCP concurrent-CRT/PD-L1 ≥1% indications.

regimen_profiles.clinical_summary: First-line ES-SCLC chemo-immunotherapy: PD-L1 blockade with carboplatin/etoposide induction followed by atezolizumab maintenance.
regimen_profiles.component_rationale: Atezolizumab: Atezolizumab is an antibody against PD-L1, a signal that can reduce an immune cell’s activity. Blocking that signal can help immune cells attack cancer. It works differently from chemotherapy. The same immune activation can inflame healthy organs, so new symptoms need assessment even when they look like ordinary treatment tiredness or a minor infection. IV and SC formulations use different doses but both carry immune risks. Carboplatin: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that interfere with copying and repair. This helps stop dividing cancer cells but also affects healthy tissues such as bone marrow. Kidney function is used to calculate its dose. It is given during the four-cycle induction phase and stops before atezolizumab-only maintenance. Etoposide: Etoposide interferes with topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps manage DNA during copying. DNA damage can then accumulate and stop cell division. Healthy rapidly renewing tissues can also be affected, explaining low blood counts, hair loss and mouth or bowel problems. Oral absorption differs from IV delivery; the prescribed oral dose must not be inferred from the IV dose.
regimen_profiles.schedule_context: Induction: atezolizumab and carboplatin on Day 1, with etoposide on Days 1–3, repeated every 21 days for up to four cycles. Maintenance: carboplatin and etoposide stop; atezolizumab alone continues every 21 days while appropriate. The fourth cycle ends about 12 weeks after starting if there are no delays; maintenance has no fixed total duration in this regimen.
key_points: Four 21-day induction cycles, then atezolizumab-only maintenance every 21 days.
IV atezolizumab 1200 mg versus SC 1875 mg are explicit alternatives; separate 1680mgIV/28-day maintenance follows NCCP 00593.
IV etoposide 100 mg/m² Days 1–3 versus IV Day 1 then 100 mg/m² PO twice daily Days 2–3; never convert silently.
Immune attribution, named-event grade, recurrence and restart context matter.
Platelets 50–<75 are unassigned in Table 5; etoposide non-dialysis CrCl<10 is unassigned in Table 6.
NCCP gives no atezolizumab dose-reduction scheme; hold or discontinue as specified.

Myocarditis, myositis and myasthenia gravis can overlap. If one is suspected, assess for the other syndromes; apply the most stringent applicable event-specific action. Suspected myocarditis requires withholding and prompt cardiology work-up; diagnosed Grade 2 or higher requires permanent discontinuation.

patient_education: Carboplatin has a high sickness risk. Your prescription usually includes several anti-sickness medicines with some doses on later days. Follow the written plan even if you initially feel well; contact the team if it is not effective.

The team should account for each chemotherapy day and for two days after the last dose. The later-day plan may overlap the medicines already started on Day 1, so obtain one clear schedule and do not add duplicate doses. Confirm the plan for oral etoposide separately.

When only atezolizumab remains, routine chemotherapy anti-sickness steroids and other prophylaxis are not automatically continued. Keep any individual rescue or hormone-replacement plan and the immunotherapy alert card. Do not stop prescribed long-term steroids yourself.

route_and_duration: Day 1 order: atezolizumab, carboplatin, then etoposide. Atezolizumab IV first infusion is 60 minutes, later 30 minutes if tolerated; SC injection takes about 7 minutes.
